title: Repent or Perish, a Woman Set Free, and the Narrow Door
summary: Told of Galileans killed by Pilate and of eighteen crushed by a falling tower, Jesus denies that the victims were worse sinners and calls his hearers to repent, then tells of a barren fig tree given one more year. On the Sabbath he frees a woman bent over for eighteen years, compares the kingdom to mustard seed and leaven, warns that many will find the narrow door shut, and, warned about Herod, laments over Jerusalem, which kills the prophets.
story: Chapter 12 ended with a call to read the present time and settle accounts before it is too late. This chapter presses the same urgency. News of disaster becomes a summons to repentance; a fig tree lives on borrowed time; the door of the kingdom will not stay open forever. Luke reminds us in verse 22 that Jesus is still making his way toward Jerusalem, and the chapter ends there in spirit, with Jesus' lament over the city that will reject him. Between the warnings stands the healing of a bent woman, a picture of what the kingdom does: it releases those Satan has bound.
historical:
The killing of Galileans in the temple courts, their blood mixed with the animals they had brought to sacrifice, is not recorded outside Luke. It fits what Josephus tells of Pilate, who used force against Jewish crowds more than once, for example when protesters objected to his use of temple funds to build an aqueduct, and who was eventually recalled to Rome in AD 36 after a massacre of Samaritans at Mount Gerizim. Galileans traveled to Jerusalem for the festivals and had a reputation for unrest, so a clash at Passover is plausible. The tower of Siloam probably stood near the Pool of Siloam in the southern part of Jerusalem; its collapse is otherwise unknown.

The Pharisees' warning about Herod Antipas (verse 31) shows that not all Pharisees were hostile to Jesus. Antipas had already executed John, so the danger was real. Parallels to parts of this chapter are found in Matthew 13:31-33, Mark 4:30-32, Matthew 7:13-14 and 7:22-23, Matthew 8:11-12, and Matthew 23:37-39. The fig tree parable, the healing of the bent woman, and the reply to Herod are found only in Luke.
cultural:
Many in the ancient world, including some in Israel, assumed that sudden disaster revealed hidden sin; the friends of Job argued this way, and the disciples asked a similar question about a man born blind (John 9:2). Fig trees were often planted in vineyards; the image of Israel as God's vineyard or fig tree from which he seeks fruit appears in the prophets (Isaiah 5:1-7, Micah 7:1). A fig tree normally bore fruit within a few years of planting, so three years of nothing meant something was wrong.

Pharisaic and later rabbinic teaching allowed necessary care for animals on the Sabbath, including leading them to water, which gives force to Jesus' argument. Calling the woman a daughter of Abraham gave her a place of honor in the covenant people; the phrase is rare. The mustard seed was proverbially tiny, and the plant could grow into a shrub taller than a man. Three measures of flour was a very large amount, enough to feed perhaps a hundred people, the same amount Sarah baked for her heavenly visitors (Genesis 18:6). Calling someone a fox could mean he was cunning or that he was a petty, destructive nuisance, not a lion.
literary: The chapter alternates warning and good news. Two reports of disaster produce the same refrain twice, “unless you repent, you too will all perish” (3, 5), and the fig tree parable follows with its open ending: will the tree bear fruit? The healing story shows the kingdom breaking in, and the two short parables of mustard seed and leaven (18-21) describe its growth from small beginnings. The question of verse 23 about how many will be saved is turned back on the questioner: Jesus answers with a command to strive, not a number. The chapter closes with a lament that quotes Psalm 118:26, the pilgrims' psalm that the crowds will shout as Jesus enters the city (19:38). Words of binding and release tie the Sabbath healing to the Nazareth sermon's promise of release for the oppressed (4:18).

outline.t: Disasters and the call to repent
The parable of the barren fig tree
A crippled woman freed on the Sabbath
Herod the fox and the lament over Jerusalem

doctrines.note: Disaster is not proof that its victims were worse sinners, but it is a reminder that everyone stands before God and needs to repent. The fig tree parable adds that God's patience gives time, but not unlimited time.

The kingdom begins small and hidden, like a seed or a pinch of leaven, and grows until it fills everything. It gathers people from east, west, north, and south to the feast with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Jesus refuses the simple equation that suffering equals special guilt. The woman's disability is linked to Satan's binding, not to her own sin, and Jesus treats her release as the Sabbath's true purpose.

words.note: Metanoeo, to repent. Repeated in verses 3 and 5, it calls the hearers to turn from their own ways to God, rather than speculating about the guilt of others. The verb form of the repentance John preached in 3:3.

Agonizomai, to strive or struggle, from the language of athletic contest (the source of the English agonize). Entering the narrow door is not effortless; it calls for earnest, wholehearted response now, while the door is open.

Deo, to bind or tie. Jesus plays on the word: people untie their animals on the Sabbath, so should not this woman, whom Satan bound, be untied? The Sabbath, which celebrated God's rest and Israel's release from Egypt, is the fitting day for release.

christ: The chapter reveals Jesus as the one who frees the bound and gathers the scattered, and as the prophet who must die in Jerusalem. His reply to Herod shows that no king controls his path; he will finish his work and on the third day reach his goal, a phrase that points beyond the literal days toward his death and resurrection. His lament over Jerusalem uses an image the Old Testament applies to God: sheltering under the wings (Psalm 91:4, Ruth 2:12). Jesus speaks of longing, many times, to gather Jerusalem's children, as if he has been the one sending the prophets all along. That longing, met with refusal, will end in tears as he approaches the city (19:41) and in the cross, where the gathering of all peoples will be accomplished.

hard.q: If the victims of Pilate and the tower were not worse sinners, why does Jesus say his hearers will perish unless they repent?
hard.a: Jesus refuses two opposite errors. He rejects the idea that tragedy is a precise measure of guilt, which would let the survivors feel safe and righteous. But he also refuses to let the tragedy become merely a sad story; it becomes a reminder that death comes to everyone and that all need to be ready. Some interpreters hear a specific warning in the phrase you too will all perish: in AD 70, Roman armies destroyed Jerusalem, and many died by the sword and under falling walls, much as the Galileans and the eighteen had. If Israel continued on the road of violent resistance and refused Jesus' way of peace, it would meet that end. Others take the warning chiefly as spiritual, about final judgment. Both readings may be intended. Either way, Jesus directs the question from why they suffered to what his hearers must do, and the fig tree parable that follows shows that God's patience is real and is meant to lead to repentance.

questions: When you hear of a disaster, do you tend to look for someone to blame? How does Jesus redirect that instinct?
The kingdom starts as small as a mustard seed. Where might God be doing something small in your life or community that you have been tempted to overlook?
Jesus longed to gather Jerusalem, but it was unwilling. What in you is unwilling to be gathered?
